RagShortTexts: Backed by Pope and Emperor, Teutonic Knights waged ruthless Baltic crusades, planting.

Variants.Content: Papal and imperial sanction gave the Order its Baltic war, and the Golden Bull of Rimini of 1226 gave them a legal claim to lands not yet conquered. After absorbing the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1237, the Order drove the Northern Crusades across Prussia, Livonia, and Estonia. Its war economy ran on tithes, tolls, and colonist labor clearing forest for farms. Red-brick Ordensburg fortresses at river crossings served as bases for raids, tax collection, and monastic administration. Yet the bishops of Riga and Dorpat resented the Order's privileges, and constant campaigns against Lithuanian and Samogitian forces drained silver and manpower each season.

The Grand Master answers only to Christ and the Pope. Under Anno von Sangershausen, the Order converts pagan marshes into disciplined German bailiwicks, extracting grain tithes and extinguishing indigenous rebellion under holy vows of poverty, chastity, and war.

Brother-knights in white mantles drive lances into Baltic skirmishers at the head of the wedge. Behind them come German crossbowmen and sergeants with pollaxes, who clear forest edges and cut down the pagan ambush zones. Keep your shield tight to your side in the thicket, watch the sergeant's hand signal, and never break ranks to chase a fleeing rider.

Prussian villagers are dragged by monks to rivers for forced baptism, their sacred oaks felled to fuel monastery lime kilns. Beneath stone keeps, pagan serfs whisper ancient chants to Perkūnas in the forest gloom.
